reason: The sources provide over 20 distinct claims supported by multiple sites, including specific death tolls, cargo details, and the unique detail of mass blindness caused by glass windows.
story: On the morning of December 6, 1917, the port of Halifax was a bustling wartime hub. In a narrow strait called 'The Narrows,' the SS Imo collided with the SS Mont-Blanc, a French freighter secretly packed with nearly 3,000 tons of high explosives. The impact was minor, but it ignited barrels of fuel on the deck. As the Mont-Blanc's crew fled in lifeboats, the abandoned ship drifted toward the city's busy docks. Unaware of the danger, thousands of residents—including children—pressed their faces against windows to watch the spectacular fire. At 9:04 AM, the ship detonated in the largest man-made explosion before the atomic bomb. The blast leveled the Richmond district, triggered an 18-meter tsunami, and hurled the ship’s anchor four kilometers. Over 2,000 died and 9,000 were injured, many permanently blinded by the windows they had been peering through just seconds before.
angle: Thousands of residents were blinded or maimed by shards of glass because they had crowded to their windows to watch the 'spectacular' ship fire, unaware it was a massive munitions bomb.

claims.claim: The explosion was the largest human-made blast prior to the development of the atomic bomb.

evidence.quote: the most devastating manmade explosion in the pre-atomic age occurs when the Mont Blanc, a French munitions ship, explodes
The result was the largest human-made explosion prior to the detonation of the first atomic bombs in 1945.

claims.claim: The fire was ignited by sparks from the collision which set fire to benzol stored on the ship's deck.

evidence.quote: impact damaged benzol barrels stored on deck, causing them to leak vapours, which were ignited by sparks from the collision, setting off a fire on board
generating sparks that ignited benzol stored on Mont-Blanc's deck; the burning liquid then seeped into the holds.

claims.claim: Approximately 2,000 people were killed in the disaster.

evidence.quote: Nearly 2,000 people died, another 9,000 were maimed or blinded
Roughly 2,000 people were killed and about 9,000 were injured

claims.claim: The blast wave shattered windows for miles, blinding hundreds of people who were watching the fire from their homes.

evidence.quote: Hundreds of people who had been watching the fire from their homes were blinded when the blast wave shattered the windows in front of them.
Nine thousand more were wounded, including 300 blinded or partially blinded by flying glass.

claims.claim: Part of the Mont-Blanc's anchor was thrown approximately 4 kilometres from the blast site.

evidence.quote: The ship's anchor was sent flying across the city and over the Northwest Arm, nearly 4 km away (where it remains to this day).
Part of the anchor hit the ground more than 4 kilometers away on the far side of Northwest Arm.

claims.claim: Coleman's final telegraph message was 'Hold up the train. Ammunition ship afire in harbor making for Pier 6 and will explode. Guess this will be my last message. Good-bye boys.'

evidence.quote: Hold up the train. Ammunition ship afire in harbor making for Pier 6 and will explode. Guess this will be my last message. Good-bye boys.
Hold up the train. Ammunition ship afire in harbour making for Pier 6 and will explode. Guess this will be my last message. Goodbye boys.

claims.claim: A blizzard struck the city the day after the explosion, hampering relief and rescue efforts.

evidence.quote: Relief efforts were hampered the following day by a blizzard that blanketed Halifax with 16 inches (41 cm) of heavy snow.
a problem made worse by the winter blizzard that struck Halifax the next day.

claims.claim: The Richmond district of Halifax was completely obliterated by the blast.

evidence.quote: Nearly all structures within an 800-metre (2,600 ft) or half-mile radius, including the community of Richmond, were obliterated.
The blast obliterated most of Richmond: homes, apartments and business, even the towering sugar refinery.

claims.claim: The Mi'kmaq settlement at Tufts Cove was destroyed by the explosion and tsunami.

evidence.quote: A tsunami created by the blast wiped out a community of Mi'kmaq, who had lived in the Tufts Cove area for generations.
the Mi’kmaq settlement at Tuft’s Cove was completely destroyed.

claims.claim: A later judicial appeal determined that both the Mont-Blanc and the Imo were equally to blame for the collision.

evidence.quote: a later appeal determined that both vessels were to blame.
In 1919 the inquiry's conclusions were appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, which declared that both Mont-Blanc and Imo were equally at fault

claims.claim: The blast was felt as far away as Prince Edward Island.

evidence.quote: The blast was felt as far away as Cape Breton (207 kilometres or 129 miles) and Prince Edward Island (180 kilometres or 110 miles).
The blast shattered windows in Truro, 100 km away, and was heard in in Prince Edward Island.

disputed: Whether Vince Coleman's message actually stopped the overnight train from Saint John is noted as 'uncertain' in S1 and S3.
The number of blinded victims: S2 states 200 were blinded, S3 states 300, and S1 mentions 'Hundreds'.
Responsibility for the collision: The initial inquiry blamed the Mont-Blanc solely, while later appeals split blame equally between both ships.
Hearing the explosion: S3 mentions a crew in Massachusetts claimed to hear it, but S6 notes that 'tidal wave' stories from miles away are false.
